ordering: By longest run descending. None of the 26 is unattributed.

rows_detail.proposed: ISO/IEC 42001 knows only nonconformity and sets no severity scheme; major and minor come from third-party certification practice under ISO/IEC 17021-1. Clause 6.4.8 of ISO 19011 allows grading against context and risk, quantitative or qualitative, and asks that the criteria be defined and communicated by whoever audits. Note the drafting difference: 42001 defines nonconformity itself at 3.16, where 27001 borrows the term from ISO/IEC 27000.

Clause 6.4.7 hands the auditor a judgement rather than a rule: when verification is weak, decide how much weight the information can bear as evidence. Weight, not admissibility - the question is never whether to use it but how far a conclusion built on it can reach.

Two or more management systems examined together at one auditee, in a single exercise. Clause 3.2. It is defined by what is being audited rather than by who is doing it, which is what separates it from a joint audit.

Clauses 3.15 and 3.17 keep these apart: the team conducts the audit, a technical expert supplies knowledge to it. Bringing a data scientist in to read model evaluation evidence is the intended use; letting that person audit their own team's work is not, and the definitions are where the line sits.

Scope is downstream of the role determination, because clause 4.3 builds it from the 4.1 issues and 4.1 includes which roles the organization holds. So an auditor tests the roles first: a scope excluding an activity the organization performs in a role it holds is an exclusion needing justification.

Clause 5.5.3 leaves the choice of method to whoever manages the programme, driven by the objectives, scope and criteria rather than by preference. On-site, remote or both, weighed against the risks and opportunities each brings. Annex A.1 carries the detail.

Clause 6.3.4 covers preparing what the audit will work from, and Annex A.13 the working documents themselves - checklists, sampling plans, evidence forms. Annex A.13 also sets the limit: they must not constrain the audit, which changes as evidence arrives. A checklist followed past the point it stopped fitting is the failure it warns about.

Clause 4.3 asks for the boundaries and applicability of the AI management system, built from the 4.1 issues and the 4.2 interested-party requirements. The scope is documented information - so it is something an auditor reads, not something the organization explains.

Clause 5.1 names eight things top management has to demonstrate, from establishing the AI policy and objectives through resourcing, communication and promoting improvement. Each is auditable through artifacts - decisions, budgets, agendas, actions taken on findings - rather than through attitude, which is what makes leadership a testable clause.

Clause 7.3 fixes what people working under the organization's control must be aware of: the AI policy, what their work contributes, and what failing to conform implies. Clause 7.4 asks the organization to decide what it communicates, when, to whom and how. Awareness is about the individual; communication is about the plan.

Not a weak nonconformity. Clause 3.11 Note 2 and clause 6.4.8 treat it as what an auditor records when the criteria ARE met and something could still be better. Grading a finding down to an opportunity because it would be awkward to raise is the misuse the distinction exists to prevent.

Clause 3.8 Note 1 observes that where the criteria are legal, statutory or regulatory, findings tend to be written as compliance and non-compliance rather than conformity. It is a note about usage, not a rule about wording, and nothing turns on which pair an auditor picks.

Clause 7.2 runs the same four steps for an AIMS as for any management system: determine the competence the work needs, confirm people hold it through education, training or experience, act and check where they do not, and keep documented evidence. The scope is anyone whose work affects AI performance, which reaches wider than the AI team.

When a tool chooses which records the auditor sees, the tool has made the sampling decision - and clause 4.7 ties sampling directly to how much confidence the conclusions can carry. The auditor still owns the conclusion, so the selection logic becomes something to understand rather than accept.

Clause 6.4.3 gives it three jobs: confirm everyone agrees the plan, introduce the team and what each person does, and check the planned activities can actually happen. Formality scales with the audit - for a routine internal one it can be no more than saying the audit is starting and what it involves.

Clause 6.4.2 assigns both roles and keeps both outside the audit. A guide opens doors, arranges interviews and clarifies; an observer watches. Neither audits, and neither should shape what the audit finds - which is the point of naming them at all.

Clause 9.3.2 names audit results as a required input to management review, alongside nonconformity and corrective action trends and monitoring results. So internal audit is not an end in itself: a management review record that does not reflect what the audits found leaves that element of 9.3.2 unevidenced.

Clause 5.4.4 counts information and communications technology among the resources a programme needs, not just people and time. A programme planned without the tooling to reach the evidence has been under-resourced in a way the schedule will not show.

Clauses 3.13 and 3.14 keep the requester and the audited apart, and a note records that in an internal audit one organization can be both - or the programme manager can be the client. The roles stay distinct even when one body fills them all, and knowing who requested the audit is how the auditor knows who the report is owed to.

Clause 4.4 frames due professional care as diligence plus judgement, and calls reasoned judgement across all situations the important part. Because ISO 19011 guides rather than requires, and ranks no principle above another, a genuine tension resolves in the auditor's reasoning and not in a rule they can point to. Annex A.3 carries more.

Clause 5.3 is about risks TO the audit, not the auditee's own: planning, resources, team selection, communication, implementation, records and their control, monitoring. The programme manager identifies them and puts them to the audit client while the programme and its resourcing are being set.

Clause 3.6 defines the extent and boundaries of an audit, noting that this usually covers locations physical and virtual, functions, units, activities, processes and the period. For an AIMS audit the virtual locations and the specific AI systems matter as much as the org chart, and a scope naming neither cannot be tested against a finding later.

Annex A.17 a) asks for interviews with people at the levels and functions actually doing the work in scope. For an AIMS that means whoever prepares data, evaluates models or runs the system - not only the manager who can describe how it is supposed to go. Interviewing upward produces the design rather than evidence of the practice.

Annex A.14 leaves the sources to the audit's scope and complexity: interviews, observation, documented information, records, summaries, reports from elsewhere. The choice follows the question - a summary answers something different from the record it summarises, and treating them as interchangeable is how an audit concludes more than it examined.

Annexes C and D of ISO/IEC 42001 are informative - C on potential AI-related objectives and risk sources, D on using the AIMS across domains and sectors. Informative means they inform and impose nothing, so no finding can rest on either. Annex A and Annex B are the normative ones.

Clause 4.5 asks for discretion over information acquired during the audit, which pulls against the completeness clause 4.3 wants - sharply where evidence holds personal data or commercially sensitive model detail. Nothing in the text ranks the two. The usual resolution is to state the finding fully and keep the underlying evidence in the audit record rather than the distributed report.
